0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel." John Calvin wrote that "when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture." Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over fourteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his apostolic ministry — probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, the sovereign purposes of God in election and in the mystery of Israel, and the shape of the redeemed life in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel's own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity — pagan, moralist, and Jew — stands guilty before the righteous God, with no resources of its own to secure acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin's magisterial commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller's Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with one of the most carefully crafted sentences in ancient literature — a single Greek sentence spanning seven verses, in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel, and his Lord with the precision of a theologian and the ardour of a man in love with what he believes. By the time the chapter ends, the same pen that wrote of the gospel as "the power of God for salvation" has traced the terrifying arc of divine wrath against human idolatry. These two things belong together: the good news is only truly good when the bad news is truly bad.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. Paul establishes the gospel (vv. 1–17), then demonstrates the need for it (vv. 18–32). The power of God for salvation is proportionate to the depth of human lostness — and that depth, as Paul will show, is vertiginous. The world Paul describes in vv. 18–32 is not ancient history; it is every human culture that has suppressed the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's opening sentence is a controlled explosion of theology. In seven verses he identifies himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God — a gospel promised in the Old Testament Scriptures, concerning God's Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead. Every phrase is a chapter of theology waiting to be unfolded. This is not a man warming up; this is a man who knows exactly what he believes and why it matters.

The word that unlocks everything is euangelion — gospel. It meant, in the first-century Roman world, the proclamation of good news, typically the accession of a new emperor or a great military victory. Paul seizes the word and repurposes it entirely. The great news is not that Caesar has triumphed; it is that Jesus Christ, Son of God, Lord, has been raised from the dead and now reigns over all things. This is a message with empire-shaking implications — which is precisely why Paul is eager to preach it in Rome itself.

The address of grace and peace — "to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints" — is not a formality. It is a theological declaration. These people, in the capital of pagan power, are loved by God. They are called. They are saints — not by virtue of their moral achievement but by virtue of their union with Jesus Christ who is holy, and who has made them holy in Him. Before Paul preaches a word of gospel to them, he speaks a word of gospel over them. This is the Pauline method: ground identity before applying imperatives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Pauline Gospel

One of the most important features of Romans 1:1–4 is Paul's insistence that the gospel he preaches was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." The gospel is not a Pauline invention or a Gentile innovation — it is the fulfilment of Israel's own scriptures. Jesus is the descendant of David (2 Samuel 7), declared Son of God by resurrection (Psalm 2). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. Any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's designation of himself as a doulos — slave — of Christ Jesus was shocking in a world where slavery was degradation. He inverts the social order: the highest dignity available to a human being is not freedom but bondage to Jesus Christ. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy above all things, the Christian claim that the best possible life is one of radical submission to Christ still provokes the same offence — and still offers the same liberation to those who discover that the lordship of Christ is the only yoke that is easy and the only burden that is light.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God... — Romans 1:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three self-descriptions in one breath: servant (slave), called apostle, set apart. The first expresses total ownership — Paul belongs to Christ as property. The second expresses sovereign commission — he did not choose this role; it was laid on him on the Damascus road. The third expresses singular purpose — like Jeremiah set apart from the womb, Paul has been reserved for this one thing: the gospel. Everything else in his life is subordinate to this central calling.

The gospel Paul describes is rooted in history (Jesus descended from David), confirmed by power (declared Son of God by resurrection), and mediated through his own apostolic office. These are not free-floating spiritual experiences; they are anchored in datable, locatable, flesh-and-blood events. The resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead is the hinge on which all of Paul's theology — and all of history — turns.

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations... — Romans 1:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The obedience of faith" — a phrase that brackets the entire letter (appearing again in 16:26) — is one of the most debated expressions in Romans. It means, most naturally, the obedience that consists in faith: the act of believing the gospel is itself the primary act of obedience to God. Faith is not passive; it is the most demanding act of the will, because it requires the surrender of self-reliance and the casting of oneself entirely on another.

The scope of the mission is universal: "all the nations" — all the Gentiles. Rome sits at the heart of the Gentile world. Paul is not visiting a church out of curiosity; he is a missionary with a mandate, writing to enlist the Roman church as a base for his westward advance. The letter is simultaneously theological masterwork and missionary strategy document.

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Loved by God" — passive voice. These people did not love their way into God's favour; they were loved before they did anything. The Reformation understanding of grace is here in seed: the initiative is entirely divine. They are also "called to be saints" — not aspiring to be saints, not trying to become saints, but already saints by virtue of the call of God that placed them in Christ. Their sainthood is not a moral category; it is a relational one.

Grace and peace — the signature Pauline greeting. Grace (charis) is the undeserved favour of God; peace (shalom) is the comprehensive well-being that results when the war between humanity and God has been ended by the blood of the cross. Paul pronounces both over his readers before he has written a single sentence of argument. The gospel is gift before it is demand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his gospel and his greeting, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians unceasingly. He has longed to visit them. He has been prevented — more than once. This passage is often passed over quickly on the way to the theological fireworks of vv. 16–17, but it deserves careful attention: it shows us what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like. Paul's longing is not merely strategic (Rome as a missionary base) but personal. He wants to see them, to be mutually encouraged, to share with them some spiritual gift.

The phrase "I am under obligation" (v. 14) — literally "I am a debtor" — is startling. Paul does not feel that preaching the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, is above and beyond the call of duty. He feels indebted to them. They have a claim on him. The grace that was lavished on him on the Damascus road was not for his private enrichment; it was for their benefit. He owes them what he received for free. This is the logic of all gospel ministry: grace received creates obligation discharged.

"I am not ashamed of the gospel" (v. 16) — the Greek construction implies the opposite: he is eagerly proud of it, itching to proclaim it in Rome's very centre. Rome was the most intimidating platform imaginable: the seat of empire, the crossroads of civilization, the city that had crucified the Lord of the gospel. And Paul cannot wait to get there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 reveals that Paul's missionary strategy is inseparable from his pastoral affection. He does not view the Roman church as an audience for his theology or a resource for his mission; he views them as beloved brothers and sisters in whom he longs to rejoice. Reformed missiology has always insisted that mission and church are inseparable — the mission proceeds from the church, through the church, and for the establishment of the church. Paul's eagerness to visit Rome exemplifies this: he is not a lone-ranger evangelist but an apostle embedded in the body of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's sense of debt to all people — Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish — erased every cultural and social hierarchy. The gospel belonged to no class or culture. Now: The contemporary church is perpetually tempted to preach a gospel shaped for those who are already culturally similar to us. Paul's "debtor" language is a rebuke: the gospel is owed to every person in our reach, regardless of whether they seem like likely converts or comfortable neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. — Romans 1:8
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Roman church's faith had become known throughout the empire — not through a communications strategy but through the organic witness of a community whose transformed lives were visible. Paul's thanksgiving is striking: he thanks God for their faith, not their achievements. Faith is itself the gift for which the giver deserves the thanks. This is grace from first to last.

"God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son" — Paul's prayer life was not compartmentalized from his ministry life. His intercession for Rome was woven into his apostolic service. He did not wait until he arrived to begin his ministry to them; he had been ministering to them on his knees for years. Prayer is the advance work of all genuine ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine. — Romans 1:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul catches himself. He begins with the apostolic confidence of one who has something to give ("that I may impart to you some spiritual gift"), then immediately corrects the impression of apostolic condescension: "that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith." The correction is theologically significant: even the apostle Paul expected to receive from those to whom he ministered. The body of Christ has no passengers.

Martyn Lloyd-Jones saw in this the model of all genuine Christian fellowship: not the expert dispensing to the novice, but believers of different gifts and experiences strengthening one another in the faith they share. The Roman Christians — some of whom had known Christ longer than Paul had — had things to give him that he needed.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Greeks and barbarians" was the first-century way of saying everyone. Greeks were the cultured, literate, philosophically sophisticated world; barbarians were everyone else — those who spoke languages that sounded to Greek ears like "bar-bar" (hence the name). Paul's gospel has no cultural prerequisites. The sophisticated Athenian philosopher and the rough Scythian tribesman stand equally in need of the same grace, and are equally capable of receiving it.

The eagerness Paul expresses for Rome is not the excitement of tourism. It is the urgency of a man who knows that people in Rome are perishing without the gospel and that he has been entrusted with the one message that can save them. Spurgeon used to say that if he believed what he claimed to believe about heaven and hell, he would crawl on his knees across broken glass to preach the gospel. Paul's eagerness for Rome has that quality.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two verses. The entire letter in miniature. Everything Paul will argue across sixteen chapters is compressed here with the density of a diamond. "I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" This is the thesis statement of Romans, and it is the sentence that changed the world.

Martin Luther, tormented by the phrase "the righteousness of God" — understanding it as the terrifying standard by which God condemns sinners — wrestled with it until the light broke. "At last," he wrote, "meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates." The Reformation began in these two verses.

The gospel is power — not advice, not inspiration, not a moral framework, but the very power of God actively at work to save. It is power for salvation — not merely forgiveness of past sins, but the complete rescue of a human being from the dominion of sin and death and the wrath of God, and the restoration of that person to the full flourishing of life in God. And it is for everyone who believes — the one condition, the one instrument, the one hand that receives what God freely gives: faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed exegesis has understood "the righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that originates with God and is given by God to the believing sinner — what the Reformers called iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, a righteousness that is not our own. Luther's breakthrough was recognising that this righteousness is not the demanding standard that condemns but the gracious gift that saves. This is the doctrine of imputation: Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to the account of the believing sinner, so that God can be simultaneously just (the sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the "wonderful exchange" — Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther's discovery of Romans 1:17 broke the back of a system of salvation by merit and religious performance that had enslaved Western Christendom for centuries. The Reformation was, at its heart, a rediscovery of these two verses. Now: Every generation re-erects the system of merit that the gospel demolishes. Every human heart, left to itself, believes it must earn its standing with God. Romans 1:16–17 is the permanent, repeatable antidote: the gospel is not something you do; it is something done for you, received by faith, given by the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Not ashamed" — the negation suggests the real possibility of shame. In Rome, where power was measured in legions and the crucified Messiah was foolishness to the Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, the gospel was not a prestigious thing to be associated with. Paul's confidence is not bravado; it is grounded in what the gospel actually is: the power of God. He is not ashamed of a philosophy or a programme; he is not ashamed of the active, saving, transforming power of the living God working through ordinary preaching.

The order "Jew first and also Greek" is not merely historical courtesy. It reflects the covenant structure of redemption: God's saving purposes moved through Israel to reach all nations. The Messiah came as Israel's king. The gospel was first preached in Jerusalem. But the first is not the only, and the covenant with Abraham always had the nations in view. The gospel has no ethnic restrictions; it has one condition only — faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
"From faith for faith" — a phrase that has generated enormous debate. Most likely it means that the righteousness of God is received by faith from beginning to end: not faith at the entry point followed by works for maintenance, but faith all the way down, from first to last. The Christian life does not begin in grace and continue in effort; it is grace from first to last, received by faith from first to last.

The citation from Habakkuk 2:4 is loaded with Old Testament context. Habakkuk had cried out to God about injustice and chaos, and God had answered with a promise that seemed impossibly deferred. "But the righteous shall live by his faith" — the one who trusts God in the darkness, who holds on to the promise when the evidence seems to point the other way, this person will live. Paul takes this text and places it at the heart of his doctrine of justification: the life that God gives comes to those who trust His promise, not those who earn His approval.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having announced the gospel, Paul immediately establishes why it is necessary. The gospel is good news only against the backdrop of very bad news — and the bad news Paul now delivers is as stark and unsparing as anything in Scripture. God's wrath is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. The problem is not ignorance; it is suppression. Humanity knows God — knows Him through creation, through conscience — and actively holds that knowledge down, refusing its implications, fleeing from its demands.

The structure of vv. 18–32 is a three-stage description of idolatry's logic and its consequences. First, the knowledge of God is suppressed (vv. 18–20). Then, God is exchanged for idols — images of creatures replacing the uncreated Creator (vv. 21–23). Then, God gives them up — three times that terrible phrase appears (vv. 24, 26, 28) — abandoning them to the sexual and moral dissolution that is both the consequence and the judgment of their idolatry. The wrath of God is not primarily a future event; it is a present reality, operating through the structure of a moral universe that reaps what it sows.

This passage is not a description of the worst of humanity — the serial killers and tyrants. It is a description of normal human culture operating without the restraining grace of God. The Rome to which Paul wrote would have recognised itself in these verses. So would every culture in every age. So would every human heart that is honest enough to look clearly at itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has insisted, against every attempt to soften or allegorize it, that the wrath of God is real, personal, and active. It is not merely the impersonal outworking of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), nor a primitive metaphor for natural consequences. It is the holy, settled, righteous opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts His character. Leon Morris showed definitively that in both Testaments, divine wrath is personal and purposeful — God's moral revulsion at sin, expressed in active judgment. The gospel is only fully good news when this wrath is fully real: Christ bore the wrath we deserved (3:25), and those who are in Christ are saved from the wrath to come (5:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's description of idol worship in vv. 22–23 — exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures — described the Roman religious world exactly. The pantheon of Rome was populated by humanised gods and deified emperors, all of them creatures rather than Creator. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance. We exchange the glory of God for the image of the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self, the entertained mind. Every idol is a creature thing promoted to Creator status — and Paul's analysis of the consequences (futile thinking, darkened hearts, moral dissolution) maps precisely onto what happens when any created thing is made to bear the weight only God can carry.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth. — Romans 1:18
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wrath of God is the subject of the very first theological statement Paul makes after his thesis. This is not accidental. The gospel of righteousness (v. 17) and the revelation of wrath (v. 18) stand in deliberate parallel: both are being "revealed" — the same Greek verb — in the present age. The gospel is being revealed through apostolic preaching; the wrath is being revealed through the observable consequences of human idolatry. They belong together. You cannot understand the gift until you have understood the danger from which it rescues.

"Suppress the truth" — the Greek word (katechō) means to hold down, to restrain, to keep from its natural expression. The knowledge of God is not absent from human beings; it is present but deliberately suppressed. This is Paul's doctrine of general revelation: God has made Himself known through creation (v. 20 — His eternal power and divine nature are clearly perceived), so that all human beings are without excuse. Atheism, in Paul's analysis, is not honest agnosticism; it is the determined refusal of knowledge that is inescapably present.

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. — Romans 1:21
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fall described in vv. 21–23 is not primarily moral but religious: it is the fall of worship. Humanity knew God — had the knowledge, had the evidence, had the obligation — and chose not to honour Him or thank Him. The failure of worship is the root of all other failures. Ingratitude toward God is not a minor oversight; it is the precise inversion of the creature's fundamental posture. The creature who will not receive everything as gift and return it to God as praise has disordered the most fundamental relationship in the universe.

"They became futile in their thinking" — the word mataioō means to become empty, vain, purposeless. The mind that is unmoored from God does not become more rational; it becomes less so. It loses the framework within which alone things make sense. Dostoevsky captured this: "If God does not exist, everything is permitted" — and nothing has meaning. The darkness of the foolish heart is not stupidity; it is the spiritual blindness that results from wilfully turning from the one true light.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonouring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen. — Romans 1:24–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first "giving over" (v. 24) is to sexual impurity — the dishonouring of the body. The connection between idolatry and sexual disorder is not accidental; it is structural. When the vertical relationship with God is disordered, the horizontal relationships between human beings inevitably follow. The person who exchanges the Creator for the creature will eventually exchange the God-given pattern of human sexuality for something that mirrors that fundamental inversion. The disorder below reflects the disorder above.

"They exchanged the truth about God for a lie" (v. 25) — the precise parallel to v. 23 (exchanging the glory of God for images). The lie is not primarily a false proposition about God; it is the false orientation of the whole life away from God and toward created things. Worship is always the issue at the root. And when worship is misdirected, the consequences flow down into every dimension of human existence — including the body and its desires.

verseByVerse.quote: They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless. — Romans 1:29–31
verseByVerse.commentary:
The catalogue of vices in vv. 29–31 is among the most comprehensive in the New Testament — twenty-one distinct moral failures, ranging from murder to gossip, from sexual disorder to disobedience to parents. The range is deliberate: Paul is not describing the worst of humanity's worst moments but the ordinary texture of human life lived without God. The murderer and the gossip are different in degree, not in kind; both are expressions of the same fundamental orientation of the self against God and neighbour.

Verse 32 is the most chilling: those who do these things not only do them but "give approval to those who practise them." The final stage of moral decay is not merely doing evil but celebrating it — building cultures and communities that honour what God forbids, that call darkness light and light darkness (Isaiah 5:20). The person who sins alone is one thing; the person who creates a social world in which sin is normalised, celebrated, and enforced has reached the depth that Paul's argument has been driving toward. This is the world without God: not merely broken but self-congratulatory about its brokenness.

2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a catalogue of Gentile vice that a first-century Jewish reader would have heard with satisfaction, nodding along at the depravity of the pagan world. Chapter 2 turns without warning on that same reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges." The trap is sprung. The person who condemns the sins of others while practising the same things is not morally superior to the Gentile; he is, Paul argues, in an even more culpable position — because he knows better.

Paul's target in chapter 2 is not the pagan but the moralist — specifically, the Jewish moralist who believes that covenant membership and religious privilege provide a buffer against divine judgment. They do not. God's judgment is impartial: He renders to each according to his works, to Jew and Gentile alike. The Gentile who has only the law of conscience will be judged by that; the Jew who has the law of Moses will be judged by that. In either case, the verdict will be the same: all fall short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rhetorical brilliance of Romans 2:1 is breathtaking. Paul has spent fourteen verses describing the moral ruin of the Gentile world — and now he wheels on the approving reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practise the very same things." The knife Paul had been pointing at the Gentile he now turns on anyone who imagines that moral judgment of others places them above judgment themselves.

The principle Paul establishes is foundational: God's judgment is according to truth (v. 2), according to works (v. 6), without partiality (v. 11). These three principles together demolish every form of religious self-satisfaction. "According to truth" means God sees through performance to reality. "According to works" means the whole life is the evidence, not merely the religious moments. "Without partiality" means no ethnic or covenant privilege exempts anyone from accountability before the Judge of all the earth.

Verses 14–15 introduce the remarkable teaching about the conscience as a moral witness — Gentiles who do not have the Torah nonetheless "show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." This is Paul's doctrine of moral general revelation: human beings are not morally blank. The conscience, however distorted by sin, retains something of the moral law written at creation. This is why all human beings, without exception, will have no excuse on the day of judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 appears to teach salvation by works — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, he will give eternal life." Reformed exegesis has understood this as describing the principle of judgment (God will judge the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). The person who truly seeks God from the heart will be given — by grace — the faith that produces the works that evidence genuine conversion. Works are the evidence of salvation, never its ground. Paul is not contradicting 1:16–17; he is establishing the standard of divine judgment that makes grace necessary for everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in covenant privilege — circumcision, Torah, temple — as a buffer against divine judgment was a live pastoral issue in Paul's day. Many Jews believed that while Gentiles might face judgment, the covenant people were secure by virtue of their membership. Paul demolishes this with surgical precision. Now: The equivalent today is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership, or moral respectability as a substitute for genuine faith and repentance. Paul's word is the same: God is not impressed by religious credentials. He is looking for the transformed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practise the very same things. — Romans 2:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word "therefore" connects chapter 2 directly to chapter 1. The person who reads chapter 1 and says "Yes! Look at those pagans!" has walked into the trap. Paul's "therefore" means: given everything I just said about human sinfulness and divine wrath, you — the moral judge, the religious observer — are equally implicated. The very act of judgment proves the presence of a moral standard; the practice of the judged sins proves the same corruption of the judge.

Jesus had said the same thing in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:1–5): the person who attends to the speck in his brother's eye while ignoring the log in his own is guilty of the very thing he condemns. Moral self-satisfaction is the most dangerous form of sin because it is the hardest to see. The person who knows she is a sinner can be brought to repentance; the person who is certain she is righteous has no need of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: He will render to each one according to his works: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, he will give eternal life... — Romans 2:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's judgment is according to works — not according to religious affiliation, ethnic identity, or moral self-assessment. This is simultaneously terrifying and fair. No one will be able to stand before the judgment seat and say they were judged by a standard they did not know; no one will be able to claim that their covenant membership exempted them from scrutiny of the life they actually lived.

"For God shows no partiality" (v. 11) — this principle, rooted in Deuteronomy 10:17 and repeated throughout the Old Testament, is here applied universally: Jew and Gentile, religious and irreligious, moral and immoral, stand before the same Judge, assessed by the same standard. The ground is level at the foot of the cross — and equally level at the bar of divine judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 12–13 state the principle of impartiality with logical precision: the standard of judgment fits the revelation received. The Gentile who sinned without the Mosaic law will be judged by the law written on his conscience; the Jew who sinned with the Torah in his hands will be judged by the Torah. Neither gets a pass. The Gentile cannot claim ignorance of all moral reality; the Jew cannot claim exemption by covenant membership.

"It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers." The implied conclusion is devastating: if righteousness requires doing, not merely hearing, and if no one does the law perfectly, then no one achieves righteousness by the law. The standard Paul sets — perfect obedience — is the very standard that will drive the argument toward the gospel: righteousness must come from outside us, because no one is righteous by their own doing.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. — Romans 2:14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's teaching on conscience here is one of the foundations of natural law theory in the Christian tradition. Even without the Torah, Gentiles possess a moral awareness — an inner witness that commends what aligns with God's law and accuses what violates it. This conscience is not infallible; sin has distorted it. But its very existence testifies to the God who wrote His moral character into the structure of human nature at creation.

The practical implication for mission is significant: the gospel can be preached to anyone because everyone already has, in some measure, the law written on their heart. The missionary does not arrive in a morally blank culture; she arrives in a culture that already knows, however dimly, that murder is wrong, that justice matters, that the weak deserve care. The gospel does not create morality from nothing; it fulfils and perfects a moral longing that God has written into every human soul.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now addresses the Jewish interlocutor directly, and the charge he levels is devastating. The Jew who possesses the Torah, who teaches it to others, who relies on it for his identity — does he keep it himself? "You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?" The indictment is not that the Torah is worthless but that it cannot save those who merely possess and teach it without obeying it from the heart.

The climax of the argument comes in the citation from Isaiah and Ezekiel: "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you." This is the ultimate indictment. Israel, entrusted with the oracles of God, called to be a light to the nations, had become in its hypocrisy a reason for the nations to despise the God of Israel. The covenant privilege had become a covenant disgrace. Nothing has changed in principle: every generation of the church must face the same charge — does our life commend the God we profess?

The solution Paul gestures toward is one of the most important concepts in the entire letter: "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (v. 29). This is the Old Testament's own vision — Deuteronomy 10:16, Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:26 — now being fulfilled in the new covenant. The mark of true belonging to God is not an outward physical sign but the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. This will be Paul's great theme in chapters 6–8.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the first extended treatment of the law's purpose and limits in the letter. Calvin identified three uses of the law: to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness in society, and to guide the redeemed life. Paul is here invoking the first use: the law reveals sin. The Jew who possesses the Torah has a clearer mirror than the Gentile — and therefore a clearer sight of his own failure to meet its demands. The law cannot save; it can only expose the need for a Saviour. This is precisely why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in circumcision as the defining covenant mark was absolute in Paul's day. To question its saving significance was to question the entire structure of Second Temple Jewish identity. Paul does not question circumcision's historical significance; he relativises it entirely: the physical sign points to a spiritual reality, and when the sign is present without the reality, it is worse than useless. Now: The equivalent is any Christian community that trusts in the outward marks of religion — baptism, church attendance, doctrinal orthodoxy, moral reputation — as substitutes for the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. Paul's word stands: God looks at the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: You then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? — Romans 2:21
verseByVerse.commentary:
The series of rhetorical questions Paul fires at his Jewish interlocutor has the effect of a prosecuting attorney working methodically through an indictment. Each question assumes its own affirmative answer: yes, you steal; yes, you commit adultery; yes, you rob temples. The charges may be representative rather than universal, but their effect is cumulative — the person who possesses the law is not thereby immune from breaking it.

The gap between what is professed and what is practised is not a new problem. It is the perennial human problem. The Pharisees of Jesus' day were not unique villains; they were vivid examples of a universal tendency. Every religious tradition, every moral code, every ethical system has its practitioners who honour its letter while violating its spirit. Paul's point is that this gap is not merely embarrassing; it is spiritually fatal — because God judges the reality, not the performance.

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? — Romans 2:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pushes the circumcision argument to its logical conclusion: the physical sign is only as good as the spiritual reality it points to. Circumcision was given as the covenant sign of a people set apart to obey God; the Jew who possesses the sign while disobeying the God of the sign has, in any meaningful sense, nullified the sign. The circumcision has become uncircumcision — the external mark is present but the covenantal reality it was meant to signify is absent.

The reversal is provocative: the uncircumcised Gentile who keeps the law's moral requirements will be counted as circumcised, while the circumcised Jew who breaks the law is effectively uncircumcised. Paul is not arguing that moral performance saves the Gentile; he is arguing that the external religious marker means nothing without the internal transformation it was always meant to represent. This prepares for vv. 28–29: the true Jew, the true circumcision, is a matter of the heart, wrought by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most theologically loaded sentences in the letter. Paul redefines Jewish identity from the inside out — not by ethnicity or ritual but by the Spirit's transforming work on the heart. He is not inventing a new category; he is completing the logic of the Old Testament itself. Deuteronomy 30:6 had promised that God would circumcise Israel's heart. Jeremiah 31 had promised a new covenant written on the heart. Ezekiel 36 had promised the gift of the Spirit to create obedience from within.

The phrase "by the Spirit, not by the letter" is not a contrast between spirit and law as such — Paul is not antinomian. It is a contrast between the outward legal requirement and the inward transforming power of the Holy Spirit who creates the obedience that the law commands but cannot itself produce. This is the new covenant reality that will be fully unveiled in chapter 8.

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 is one of the most concentrated pieces of theological argument in the entire Bible. It moves through three distinct but connected moments: the faithfulness of God despite human faithlessness (vv. 1–8), the universal verdict of guilt on the entire human race from the Old Testament's own testimony (vv. 9–20), and then — with the two most beautiful words in the letter — "But now" (v. 21): the announcement of a righteousness from God that is apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

The emotional architecture of the chapter is deliberate. Paul has spent two chapters building the case for universal human guilt — the Gentile guilty through creation and conscience, the Jew guilty despite law and covenant. Now he delivers the verdict that springs from the evidence: no one righteous, not even one. And then, from within the deepest valley of human hopelessness, he sounds the trumpet of the gospel: the righteousness of God has been manifested. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Jewish identity and covenant privilege provide no buffer against divine judgment (chapter 2), an obvious question arises: what advantage has the Jew? Was the entire covenant history of Israel pointless? Paul will not allow this conclusion. The advantage is real and great: "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." The Torah, the prophets, the promises — these are not nothing. They are the priceless repository of God's self-revelation and covenant purposes. The problem is not the oracles; the problem is the people who received them.

But what about God's faithfulness? If Israel has been faithless to the covenant, does that mean God's covenant promises have failed? Never, Paul declares — and the energy of his negation (mē genoito — "by no means!", "God forbid!", the strongest possible denial in Greek) is palpable. God's faithfulness is not contingent on human faithfulness. He remains true even when every human being is a liar. The covenant will not fail because the Covenant God cannot fail.

This brief passage anticipates the great argument of chapters 9–11: the apparent failure of Israel to embrace her Messiah does not represent a failure of God's word. His purposes stand. His faithfulness endures. The mystery of Israel's unbelief is not the defeat of God's plan but a part of it — and Paul will unfold that mystery with breathtaking scope later in the letter.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Faithfulness and Human Failure

The question of whether human sin can thwart God's covenant purposes is one of the deepest in all theology. Romans 3:3–4 gives the Reformed answer: it cannot. God's faithfulness is not a function of human response; it is grounded in His own immutable character. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. This has practical implications for Christian assurance: our standing in the covenant does not rest on our faithfulness but on God's. He who called us is faithful; He will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have been relieved by Paul's affirmation of Israel's covenant privileges, but troubled by his insistence that these privileges provide no exemption from judgment. The tension — covenant advantage, yet equal accountability — was genuinely new, though rooted in the Old Testament prophets. Now: Christians face the same tension. The advantages of covenant community — Scripture, sacrament, preaching, prayer — are real and great. They are also not saving substitutes for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability always travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, 'That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.' — Romans 3:4
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's citation of Psalm 51:4 is audacious: David, confessing his sin against Bathsheba and Uriah, acknowledges that God is justified in whatever He does — even in judging David. Paul uses this as the template for all human-divine relations. God's righteousness and truthfulness are not measured by human standards; they are the standard by which all else is measured. When God judges, He is always right, even when we cannot see it.

"Let God be true" is not a wish but an affirmation: God is true, whatever the contrary evidence appears to be. This is the foundation of Christian hope in the darkest circumstances. When God's promises seem to have failed, when prayers seem unanswered, when the covenant people seem abandoned — the Christian response is not doubt but the defiant trust of Psalm 51: God is justified. He will prevail.

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? — Romans 3:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is dealing with a sophistic objection that his gospel apparently generates: if human sin provides the dark background against which God's righteousness shines more brightly, why should God punish sin? Doesn't sin serve God's purposes? Paul dismisses this with contempt — "I speak in a human way" (v. 5) — and then anticipates the even more extreme version of the objection that will arise again in 6:1: if grace abounds where sin abounds, why not sin more?

The objection is itself a reductio of the gospel to absurdity. Paul will not dignify it with extended argument here. The person who draws this conclusion from the gospel has not understood the gospel. Grace does not make sin inconsequential; it makes sin paid for — and the price paid on the cross is the most powerful argument against sinning ever given to the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has argued the guilt of the Gentile from creation and conscience. He has argued the guilt of the moralist and the Jew from their own failure to live by the law they possess. Now he seals the case with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures. The catena of Old Testament citations in vv. 10–18 — drawn from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 — forms a comprehensive indictment: no one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God; their throats are open graves, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, their feet swift to shed blood, and there is no fear of God before their eyes.

The theological move is masterful. Paul is not importing foreign charges against Israel; he is using Israel's own sacred texts to establish Israel's own guilt. The Torah was given to the Jew; and the Torah says that no one is righteous. Therefore the Jew who trusts in the Torah as a source of righteousness has not read the Torah carefully enough. The law's purpose is not to provide righteousness but to reveal the absence of it: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20).

"No one" — the universality is relentless. Not most people. Not unreformed people. Not people without religion. No one. The scope of the verdict prepares for the scope of the remedy: the gospel is for everyone because everyone needs it equally. There are no moral high achievers who need it slightly less. There are no spiritual derelicts for whom it is too late. The ground is completely level: all have sinned, all fall short (v. 23), all are justified freely by grace (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. The doctrine does not mean that every human being is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every dimension of human nature — the mind ("no one understands"), the will ("no one seeks for God"), the affections, the speech, the conduct, the very orientation of the soul. No part of the human person is untouched by the fall. This means that the human contribution to salvation is precisely zero: we do not contribute our goodwill, our moral achievement, our religious sensitivity. Salvation is entirely of God from beginning to end. This is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is "freely" given — there is nothing in us to which it could be a response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The catena of psalms and prophets Paul deploys was drawn from Israel's own worship book. These were texts sung in the temple, prayed in the synagogue, memorised by devout Jews. Their application to Israel's own guilt was deeply confrontational — like a church being indicted by its own hymns. Now: The contemporary church sometimes prefers a more optimistic anthropology — emphasising human potential and the image of God while minimising the ravages of the fall. Romans 3:9–20 is the permanent corrective. The doctrine of human depravity is not pessimism; it is realism. And realism about the disease is the precondition for gratitude for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God." — Romans 3:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Are we Jews any better off?" — the question Paul has been building toward for three chapters. The answer is given without hesitation: No, not at all. The same God who will judge Gentiles by creation and conscience will judge Jews by the Torah — and the verdict is identical: all are under sin. The phrase "under sin" (hyph' hamartian) is spatial — sin is a power, a dominion, beneath which all humanity crouches. Not merely sinful by behaviour, but subject to sin as a ruling force.

The catena of Scripture citations that follows (vv. 10–18) is Paul's most extended Old Testament quotation in Romans. He is making a formal case from Israel's own holy writings. The very texts that Israel treasured and sang in worship testify against Israel. "None is righteous, no, not one" — the universality is relentless, the source unimpeachable. Israel cannot appeal the verdict by appealing to Scripture; Scripture is the prosecution's primary evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive. The venom of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood; in their paths are ruin and misery... There is no fear of God before their eyes. — Romans 3:13–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
The catena moves anatomically downward: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes. Every organ of the human body is indicted. The throat — the passage of speech and breath — is an open grave, emanating death. The tongue deceives. The lips harbour venom. The mouth overflows with curses. The feet rush toward bloodshed. And the root of it all, stated last: no fear of God before their eyes. The eyes that do not see God rightly produce the throat, tongue, lips, mouth, and feet that behave as described.

Proverbs 1:7 says that "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." The absence of that fear is therefore the beginning of folly — not merely intellectual error but moral dissolution at the deepest level. The catalogue of vv. 13–18 is not a description of the exceptional criminal; it is the anatomy of a humanity that has lost its orientation to God and therefore lost its orientation to everything else. The diagnostic power of Scripture: it names not just what we do but what we are in ourselves, apart from grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. — Romans 3:19
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Every mouth stopped" — the image is of a courtroom where the defendant, having heard the indictment, has nothing to say. The law's function in this context is prosecutorial: it silences every human excuse, every plea of mitigating circumstances, every claim of comparative righteousness. Before God, no one can say "but I was better than most" or "consider what I did achieve." Every mouth is stopped.

"Through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20b) — this is the law's diagnostic function, which Luther and Calvin called the first use of the law. The law is a mirror, not a ladder. It shows us what we are, not how to become what we should be. The person who understands this has been prepared by the law to receive the gospel — because she has been stripped of every alternative source of righteousness and left with only the grace of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But now" — nuni de. Two words in Greek that change everything. After three chapters of unrelenting diagnosis — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the Jew convicted by his own scriptures, the entire world accountable to God — these two words open a door out of a sealed room. The righteousness of God has been manifested. Apart from the law. Through faith in Jesus Christ. For all who believe. Freely. By grace. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

This is the centre of Romans. This is the centre of Paul's gospel. This is the theological core of the Reformation. Every word of vv. 21–26 has been weighed and debated and celebrated for two millennia — and still it burns with the same fire. God put Christ forward as a propitiation — a mercy seat, a place of atonement — by His blood, to be received by faith. In this act, God demonstrated His own righteousness: He passed over former sins (under the patient forbearance of the old covenant) and He condemned the sin that deserved condemnation — in His own Son, at Calvary. The God who justifies the ungodly (4:5) is not a God who winks at sin. He is a God who bore its full weight in the person of His Son.

Boasting is excluded (v. 27). The person who is justified by faith through Christ has nothing to boast of but Christ. The Jew cannot boast in the Torah; the Greek cannot boast in philosophy; the moralist cannot boast in her record; the religious cannot boast in his devotion. The ground is level. There is one God, and He justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. The gospel is the great leveller — and the great glorifier, because it redirects all glory from the creature to the Creator.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement

Romans 3:25 introduces one of the most important words in the New Testament: hilastērion — propitiation. This word carries the specific meaning of an offering that averts divine wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris demonstrated exhaustively that this is the correct reading against C.H. Dodd's attempted substitution of "expiation" (which only removes sin, without reference to wrath). Christ's death on the cross was not merely a moral demonstration or a removal of guilt; it was the bearing of the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God could be both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). The Reformed tradition has always insisted on this: without propitiation, justification has no foundation. If the wrath was not truly satisfied, the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of vv. 24–25 deliberately echoes the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16: the mercy seat (hilastērion) where blood was sprinkled to cover the sins of the people. Paul is saying: what the Day of Atonement pointed to, Christ has accomplished — once for all, for all who believe. The entire sacrificial system of the old covenant found its fulfilment and its terminus in the cross. Now: Every human religion has some mechanism for dealing with the problem of guilt — sacrifice, ritual, moral achievement, reincarnation, denial. Romans 3:21–31 announces that the only mechanism that actually works is the one God provided: the substitutionary death of His own Son, received by faith. There is no other name, no other blood, no other righteousness that avails.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it — the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. — Romans 3:21–22
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Apart from the law" does not mean against the law or in ignorance of the law. It means apart from law-keeping as the basis of righteousness. The law and the prophets bore witness to this righteousness — it is not new; it is the fulfilment of what the entire Old Testament was pointing toward. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (chapter 4). David spoke of the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works. The gospel is the completion of the Old Testament, not its cancellation.

"For all who believe" — the phrase appears twice in rapid succession, as if Paul cannot emphasise it enough. The only condition is faith. Not faith plus works. Not faith plus ritual. Not faith plus ethnicity or moral achievement. Faith — the open hand that receives what God freely gives. This is the radical democracy of the gospel: the most learned theologian and the least educated believer stand on exactly the same ground before God.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God's righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. — Romans 3:25
verseByVerse.commentary:
God put Christ forward — the initiative is entirely divine. This is not a Son appeasing a reluctant Father; the Father Himself provides the propitiation. The love of God and the justice of God meet at the cross, not in opposition but in unity. God demonstrates His love by giving His Son (5:8); God demonstrates His justice by not passing over sin but bearing it in His Son. The cross is simultaneously the greatest act of love and the most rigorous expression of justice in the history of the universe.

"To be received by faith" — the atonement, objectively accomplished at Calvary, is subjectively received through faith. The bridge between what Christ did and what the sinner receives is faith — not as a meritorious act, but as the God-given instrument of reception. Faith does not earn the righteousness; it lays hold of it. It is the hand that takes the gift, not the labour that earns the wage.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. — Romans 3:27
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exclusion of boasting is not a moral aspiration but a logical consequence of the gospel's structure. If justification is by grace, through faith, in Christ — then there is no human contribution to be proud of. The faith itself is not a meritorious act; it is the renunciation of merit. The one who is justified by faith has nothing to boast of but the Christ who justified him — and boasting in Christ is not boasting at all; it is worship.

Paul ends the chapter by insisting that the gospel of justification by faith upholds the law rather than overthrowing it (v. 31). The law's demands have been met — not by us, but by Christ on our behalf. The law's verdict has been executed — not against us, but against Christ in our place. The law is not abolished; it is honoured, more perfectly than any human performance could ever honour it. This is the wonderful exchange: Christ honours the law in our place; we receive the verdict that His law-keeping deserved.

4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works of the law, Paul faces an immediate objection from Jewish readers: what about Abraham? Abraham is the father of the Jewish nation, the recipient of the covenant, the model of obedience. If he was justified by his works, then surely righteousness is earned, not given. Romans 4 is Paul's extended answer — and it is devastating in its exegetical precision and its theological reach.

The answer is simple and irrefutable: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 precedes Genesis 17), and before the law was given (by four centuries). The very man whom Judaism claimed as the exemplar of covenant faithfulness is in fact the exemplar of justifying faith — and therefore the father not only of circumcised Jewish believers but of all Gentile believers as well. The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's argument from Abraham is both simple and lethal to the works-righteousness position. He goes directly to Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." The verb "counted" (Greek: logizomai; Hebrew: chashab) is an accounting term — to reckon to someone's account. God reckoned Abraham righteous — not because Abraham had earned it but because Abraham believed. The righteousness was credited; it was not achieved.

Paul then deploys a second argument from David. Psalm 32:1–2 speaks of the blessedness of the man whose sins are not counted against him. David was not speaking of a man who earned God's favour; he was speaking of a man who received forgiveness he did not deserve. Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven — not whose record is clean. The whole Old Testament agrees: righteousness before God is received, not achieved.

The third and clinching argument concerns the timing of Abraham's circumcision. The justification of Genesis 15:6 precedes the circumcision of Genesis 17 by perhaps fourteen to twenty-four years. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive His righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Calvin called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.' — Romans 4:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
The citation of Genesis 15:6 is Paul's knockout punch. The verse is brief, clear, and unambiguous: Abraham believed, and God counted it as righteousness. Not: Abraham obeyed, and God rewarded him. Not: Abraham earned, and God paid the wage. The language is explicitly not that of wages (v. 4) but of gift. "To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness" (v. 5).

"Who justifies the ungodly" — this phrase is theologically explosive. The Old Testament explicitly forbids the unjust judge from "justifying the wicked" (Proverbs 17:15; Exodus 23:7). Yet God, the perfectly just Judge, justifies the ungodly. How? Not by overlooking their ungodliness but by punishing it — in Christ. The justice of God is not set aside in justification; it is satisfied. The one who justifies the ungodly is the one who sent His Son to bear the condemnation the ungodly deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: 'Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.' — Romans 4:6–8
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's second witness for justification by faith is David — and the citation from Psalm 32 adds a crucial dimension to Abraham's example. Where Abraham is the example of righteousness credited to faith, David is the example of sin not counted against the penitent. The blessing David celebrates is the blessedness of forgiveness: lawless deeds forgiven, sins covered, iniquity not reckoned. David had committed adultery and murder; the psalm he wrote afterward does not attempt to minimise these facts. It simply declares: God has not counted them against me.

The principle of non-imputation — God not counting sin against the sinner — is the negative side of the same coin as positive imputation of righteousness. In Christ, both are true simultaneously: the believer's sin is not counted against her, and Christ's righteousness is counted in her favour. David had experienced the first dimension; the full disclosure of both awaited the cross and resurrection. But the pattern was already there in Israel's psalter: God blesses not the performance-based achiever but the forgiven sinner who has cast herself on His mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised... — Romans 4:11
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision as a "sign and seal" — Paul introduces language that will become central to the Reformed theology of the sacraments. A sign points to a reality; a seal confirms and ratifies it. Circumcision pointed to and confirmed the righteousness that Abraham already had by faith. It was the visible token of an invisible reality already received. Applied to Christian baptism by the Westminster Confession and the Reformed tradition: baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, confirming to faith what is already true of the one who has believed.

The sequence — faith, then sign — is the pattern for all covenant religion. The sign does not create the reality it signifies; it confirms it. The person who treats circumcision (or baptism) as the source of the righteousness has reversed the order and missed the point entirely.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now extends his argument to the promise God made to Abraham — that he would be heir of the world, that his offspring would be numberless, that through him all nations would be blessed. This promise, Paul insists, was given through the righteousness of faith, not through the law. The law cannot be the means of inheriting the promise, because the law can only pronounce wrath (it condemns those who fail to keep it); if the promise depends on law-keeping, the promise is void for everyone.

The portrait of Abraham's faith in vv. 17–21 is one of the most moving passages in the entire New Testament. Abraham — "as good as dead" at a hundred years old, Sarah's womb "dead" — hoped against hope. He did not weaken in faith when he considered the hopeless biological reality. He did not waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that what God had promised He was also able to perform. This is faith in its purest form: not faith in the circumstances, not faith in human possibility, but faith in the God who raises the dead and calls into existence things that do not exist (v. 17).

And then the connection to us: this was written not for Abraham's sake alone but for ours — for those who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. The resurrection is not merely the proof that Jesus is who He claimed to be; it is the declaration that the justification He accomplished has been accepted. The empty tomb is God's receipt for a debt paid in full.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of His deity but the declaration that His atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in His death; it is faith in the God who raised Him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond Him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void. — Romans 4:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise God made to Abraham — that he would be heir of the world, that through him all nations would be blessed — was made four centuries before the Mosaic law was given. It therefore cannot have been conditioned on law-keeping. If the promise is only for those who keep the law, then faith is rendered empty and the promise is void for everyone — since no one keeps the law perfectly. The logic is inexorable: promise and law are two different economies, and they cannot coexist as means of the same end.

"For the law brings wrath" (v. 15) — a stark statement of the law's effect when it is treated as the means of inheriting the promise. The law cannot give life; it can only expose the failure to meet the standard it requires. Where there is no law, there is no transgression in the technical sense — no defined standard, no measured falling short. But where the law is, it creates transgression by defining the standard and revealing how far short we fall. Grace operates in a different register entirely: not defining a standard for us to meet, but giving what we cannot achieve.

verseByVerse.quote: In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, 'So shall your offspring be.' — Romans 4:18
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hope against hope" — the phrase captures the paradox of biblical faith perfectly. On the human level, there was no hope: a hundred-year-old man, a ninety-year-old woman, a promise of numberless offspring. Every natural indicator pointed to impossibility. And Abraham believed anyway. Not naively — he did not pretend the biology was favourable (v. 19). He looked at his own body and acknowledged the reality. And then he looked at God and trusted the promise over the reality.

This is the structure of all genuine Christian faith: not the refusal to look at hard realities, but the refusal to let hard realities have the final word. The cancer diagnosis is real. The broken marriage is real. The prodigal child is real. The financial ruin is real. Abraham's faith does not deny any of it — it simply insists that the God who promises is more real than all of it, and that His word is more certain than the evidence of our senses or the calculations of our reason.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith 'was counted to him as righteousness.' But the words 'it was counted to him' were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–23
verseByVerse.commentary:
The connection between Abraham's justification and ours is explicit: the Genesis text was not written merely as biography. It was written as theology — specifically, as the pattern for how God justifies all who believe. The same verb (logizomai — to count, reckon, credit) that was used of Abraham's faith being credited as righteousness is the verb used of our faith being credited. The pattern is identical because the God is identical and the mechanism is identical.

This is Paul's hermeneutical principle for reading the Old Testament: narrative is theological, history is instructive, biography is paradigmatic. The story of Abraham is not merely a chapter in the history of Israel; it is the template for understanding how any human being — in any age, of any ethnicity — stands righteous before God. By faith. Through grace. Credited, not earned. The same yesterday, today, and forever.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallelism of v. 25 is exquisite: delivered up for our trespasses — raised for our justification. Death dealt with sin; resurrection accomplished justification. The cross is where our guilt was carried; the empty tomb is where our acquittal was declared. This means that the Christian's confidence in their justification rests not merely on the death of Christ (sufficient) but on the resurrection of Christ (declared). A dead Saviour might have died for our sins, but could not justify us; a risen Saviour has been declared by God to have accomplished what He came to accomplish.

"Raised for our justification" — the resurrection is not merely apologetic (proving Jesus is Lord) but forensic (declaring the sinner righteous). When God raised Jesus from the dead, He was saying: the price has been paid; the sin has been dealt with; the one who trusts in this risen Lord is acquitted. The empty tomb is the receipt for every sin of every believer — paid, cancelled, gone.

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Romans 5 is the hinge of the letter. Behind us lie three chapters of diagnosis and one chapter of remedy; ahead lie three chapters of Christian experience and life.
